title: Best Zed Alternatives in 2026
summary: Zed alternatives compared on speed, OS support, extensions, collaboration and price: VS Code, Sublime Text, Lapce, Neovim, Helix, JetBrains and more.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Zed's Personal plan is still $0, though using Zed's own hosted models or Edit Predictions takes the $10/month Pro plan.
- Eight of the nine editors here have a $0 option, IntelliJ IDEA's free core included; Sublime Text is the one you pay for, at $99 once after a free evaluation.
- All 10 picks run on macOS, Windows and Linux, and two of them, Neovim and Helix, are terminal editors.
- Lag hurts editing more than typing: in a 31-person University of Regensburg study, correcting text took 46.5 seconds at 200 ms of latency versus 38.9 seconds at 20 ms.


Zed is the editor people pick when they want typing to feel instant: a native app with real-time multiplayer editing and an agent panel built in. It reached 1.0 on April 29, 2026, and v1.28.1 shipped on November 11.


So why look at Zed alternatives at all? Often it's one gap, such as a missing extension, thin Java tooling, Zed's hosted models moving behind a paid plan, or, in one user's report, slow loading on Windows.


This list covers nine editors and one different route, compared on what you give up by leaving Zed: speed, operating system, extensions, AI and price model. We build Awesomic, so it sits first, and its entry says plainly that it isn't an editor.


After it, the editors are grouped by type: VS Code, then the native editors Sublime Text and Lapce, the terminal editors, the full IDEs and, last, the AI-first IDEs. Prices are the ones each vendor listed when we re-checked on November 13, 2026.


## Why people look for Zed alternatives


People leave Zed for narrow, practical reasons, and each one points to a different set of Zed editor alternatives, which is why this list mixes native editors, terminal tools and full IDEs.


Extensions are the gap Zed itself documents. It has "hundreds" of them, and its own migration guide admits that "Zed does not offer as many extensions as VS Code." If your workflow depends on one niche linter or debugger, that single gap can decide the move.


Windows support is newer. Zed shipped there on October 15, 2025, and it needs a DirectX 11 GPU. One[Reddit user](https://www.reddit.com/r/ZedEditor/comments/1tgcahd/how_decent_is_zed_as_a_vscode_replacement/omhz4vi/) went back to VS Code after about three months because of startup and loading times across many small projects "at least in Windows."


The same user found both editors fast on Linux and said Zed "feels nicer," so the complaint is about Windows, and it's one person's experience.


Pricing changed too. On the free plan, "Zed's hosted models and Edit Predictions require a Pro subscription," and Pro costs $10/month. The free tier still lets you bring your own API keys for Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama and more, run external agents, and use other providers' predictions. Copilot is one provider Zed lists, and[Copilot's free tier](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/github-copilot-alternatives) caps you at 2,000 completions a month.


For companies, the gaps are about administration and language depth. Zed's Business plan costs $30/seat/month with no seat minimum, but SSO, SAML and SCIM are "planned but not currently available." Java and Kotlin teams hit a different wall: Zed's own comparison page concedes that JetBrains has the deeper tooling for those languages.


## What you trade when you leave a fast editor


Speed is why many people chose Zed, so it's worth knowing what lag costs. Schmid, Bierschneider, Hoffmann, Liu and Wimmer tested 31 participants at 20 ms and 200 ms of lag in a[2023 study on input latency](https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/55007/1/text-input-latency.pdf) , "Effects of Text Input Latency on Performance and Task Load."


Plain copy-typing barely moved, at 290.9 versus 302.7 ms per character, which wasn't significant. Correcting text took 38.9 seconds at 20 ms and 46.5 seconds at 200 ms (p < 0.001), with more effort and frustration, and an exploratory result suggests fast typers notice lag more. The study used plain text and tested lag levels, not any editor here, but fixing code means a lot of this kind of correcting.


Speed is only one of the trades, though, and each alternative below makes a different set:


- Rendering, where native editors such as Sublime Text and Lapce differ from Electron-based VS Code and from Cursor, which builds on VS Code's codebase.
- OS coverage, including ARM64 builds, terminal-only tools and browser access.
- Extensions, where VS Code's pool is far larger than Zed's and Helix has no plugin system.
- Collaboration, which Zed builds in with multiplayer editing, channels, voice and screen sharing.
- Price model, from free and open source to a one-time license or a monthly AI plan.


Collaboration is the easiest trade to miss. Teams that practice[design-driven development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/design-driven-development) review work together often, and in Zed that review can happen live, with two people editing the same file at once and no second app.

The table below puts all ten Zed alternatives side by side, with each one's operating systems in the last column.

### 2. VS Code


**Overview:** VS Code is the safe way back from Zed when an extension you need is missing. The price is speed, because its Electron shell is heavier than a native editor. In return, it runs almost anywhere, from Arm32 Linux to the browser at vscode.dev.


**Key features:**


- A far larger extension pool than Zed's, so niche linters and debuggers are usually covered.
- A choice of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Microsoft or open-weight models, or your own key, with Copilot, Claude or Codex as the agent.
- An Agents window for running several agents in parallel.


**Pricing:** The editor is free. Copilot adds AI from a Free plan with 2,000 completions a month to Pro at $10/month, Pro+ at $39 and Max at $100, with Business at $19 and Enterprise at $39 per seat.


**Pros:** free editor, a far wider extension choice than Zed, builds for Arm64 Windows and Linux


**Cons:** Electron shell, Live Share is an extension rather than built in, AI past 2,000 monthly completions costs extra


**Why it's a good Zed alternative:** It's the lowest-risk move, since your extensions and keybindings probably started here.


**Final verdict:** Go back to VS Code when one extension matters more than startup speed.


### 3. Sublime Text


**Overview:** Sublime Text keeps Zed's headline trait, a native, GPU-rendered interface, and leaves out the AI and collaboration layer. It runs natively on Apple Silicon Macs, Windows and Linux, with ARM64 builds for Linux, and sells personal licenses as a one-time purchase.


**Key features:**


- Tab Multi-Select for working across several open files together.
- TypeScript, JSX and TSX support built in, so front-end files need no setup.
- A Python plugin API, with LSP support added through a plugin, so language servers still work.


**Pricing:** You can evaluate it for free, then a Personal license costs $99 once with 3 years of updates. The license never expires, though versions released more than 3 years after purchase need a paid upgrade. Business costs $65/seat/year for the first 10 seats.


**Pros:** one key covers all your machines, ARM64 builds for Apple Silicon and Linux, a one-time personal license


**Cons:** paid after evaluation, no built-in AI agent, no real-time collaboration listed


**Where it fits:** Developers who loved Zed's speed and rarely opened its agent panel.


**Final verdict:** Sublime Text is the pick if a native editor is worth $99 once to you and you don't need built-in AI.


### 4. Lapce


**Overview:** Lapce is the closest like-for-like swap for Zed, written in pure Rust with a GPU-rendered UI. Unlike Sublime Text, it's free, under Apache-2.0, and still pre-1.0, though its repo was updated within the last two months.


**Key features:**


- Built-in remote development, so you can edit code on a server.
- Built-in modal editing, so Vim habits work without a plugin.
- WASI plugins you can write in any language, plus built-in LSP.


**Pricing:** Lapce costs nothing, and since its site lists no AI agent features, any AI comes from a separate tool.


**Pros:** free, native Rust rendering, remote development out of the box


**Cons:** small ecosystem, no AI agent features listed, pre-1.0 releases


**Why it made this list:** It keeps Zed's native Rust rendering and drops the AI layer.


**Final verdict:** Try Lapce if speed was the whole reason you used Zed and a pre-1.0 version doesn't worry you.


### 5. Neovim


**Overview:** Neovim is a terminal editor you configure in Lua, now at v0.12.6 from October 9, 2026. Zed ships its own Vim mode, so Vim users can go either way, and Neovim wins when you'd rather carry one config into any terminal.


**Key features:**


- Built-in LSP client and Tree-sitter, so language support takes config, not a plugin stack.
- A built-in terminal and multicursor editing.
- Lua plugins and Lua config, so every key and panel is yours to change.


**Pricing:** Neovim is free, so the real cost is the hours you spend on configuration.


**Pros:** free, works over SSH and tmux, runs on arm64 machines on every major OS


**Cons:** you assemble the IDE yourself, no built-in agent panel, terminal-first


**What it does better than Zed:** It runs on the server itself, inside the terminal you opened over SSH, so no local editor app has to connect to the remote machine.


**Final verdict:** Pick Neovim if you'd rather own every line of your setup than accept an editor's defaults.


### 6. Helix


**Overview:** Helix is a terminal editor built around multiple selections, and its site sums up the build in two words: "No Electron." Where Neovim asks you to assemble an IDE, Helix ships language support that needs no config files, only the language servers you install.


**Key features:**


- Multiple selections as the main way you edit, so you change many places in one pass.
- Tree-sitter highlighting and LSP support with no config files, so highlighting works right away and language features work after you install a server.


**Pricing:** Helix is free under MPL-2.0. Builds exist for Linux, macOS and Windows.


**Pros:** language support with no config files, free and open source, no Electron


**Cons:** "currently no plugin system available," no GUI, the last tagged release (25.07.1) dates from July 18, 2025


**Why Zed users shortlist it:** Anyone who used Zed's Helix mode already knows the basic key model, and the repo had fresh commits in November 2026.


**Final verdict:** Choose Helix if you want a modal terminal editor that works without config files or a plugin hunt.


### 7. JetBrains IDEs


**Overview:** JetBrains IDEs are the full-IDE trade: you give up a light editor for the deepest Java and Kotlin tooling on this list. IntelliJ IDEA 2026.3, released November 5, 2026, ships for Windows (x64, ARM64), macOS (Intel, Apple Silicon) and Linux (x64, ARM64).


**Key features:**


- CLion, DataGrip, Rider, RubyMine, RustRover and WebStorm free for non-commercial use.
- JetBrains AI as an add-on, at $100/year for AI Pro or $300/year for AI Ultimate.


**Pricing:** IntelliJ IDEA is free to download with 30 days of Ultimate included, and when the trial ends, its core Java and Kotlin features stay free. Ultimate for individuals costs $199 the first year, $159 the second and $119 from the third, billed annually, and organizations pay $719/user/year.


**Pros:** a free core IDE, a falling Ultimate price for long-term individual users, free non-commercial editions, ARM64 builds for Windows, macOS and Linux


**Cons:** per-user pricing for commercial work, a heavy IDE, AI billed separately


**Its real strength:** Java and Kotlin depth, an area where Zed's own comparison page points to JetBrains.


**Final verdict:** If your day is Java or Kotlin, JetBrains is worth the heavier IDE.


### 8. Cursor


**Overview:** Cursor's own pages say it's "based upon the VS Code codebase," so leaving Zed for it trades a native editor for VS Code's heavier base. You get back one-click import of VS Code extensions, themes, settings and keybindings, on macOS, Windows (x64, ARM64) and Linux. Cursor has been part of SpaceX since August 14, 2026, per Cursor's own post.


**Key features:**


- Cursor and Grok models on Plus, with third-party models at API list price from prepaid credit on Premium.
- Cloud agents and Bugbot on Premium.


**Pricing:** In October 2026 Cursor moved to "The X Subscription," which bundles Cursor, Grok and X: Free $0, Plus $8/month or $80 a year, Premium $30, Super $100 and Ultra $200, with Teams at $30, $100 or $200 per seat. Existing plans continue unchanged, and switching is optional.


**Pros:** an $8 monthly Plus plan, cloud agents on Premium, ARM64 builds for Windows


**Cons:** VS Code's heavier base, no third-party models or own keys on Plus, prices "subject to change"


**Where it beats Zed:** Extension coverage, because your VS Code extensions come with you.


**Final verdict:** Cursor suits you if you want AI at the center and can accept a VS Code-based editor's weight.


### 9. Google Antigravity


**Overview:** Google Antigravity comes as an IDE, an App, a CLI and an SDK, and it runs on macOS, Windows (x64, ARM64) and Linux (x64, ARM64). It's agent-first, so if editor speed is why you chose Zed, you're trading away Zed's main reason to exist.


**Key features:**


- Gemini models such as Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Hydrogen (added November 12), with unlimited Tab completions on the free Individual plan.
- Claude Sonnet and Opus 5.5 on higher Google AI plans.
- Extensions for JetBrains, Xcode and Eclipse, so the agent can follow you into another IDE.


**Pricing:** The Individual plan costs $0, with basic weekly limits, though Tab completions stay unlimited. Business runs through Gemini Enterprise, with seat plans from $30/seat/month or usage billing without seats.


**Pros:** a $0 plan with unlimited Tab completions, a CLI and SDK alongside the IDE, ARM64 builds for Windows and Linux


**Cons:** no bring-your-own-key in the IDE or App (the CLI takes only a Gemini key), agent-first rather than speed-first, weekly limits on the free plan


**Why it earns a place here:** For a Zed user who lived in the agent panel, it's a free way to keep that habit.


**Final verdict:** Try Antigravity if the agent mattered more to you than the editor around it.


### 10. Devin Desktop


**Overview:** Devin Desktop is Cognition's editor, renamed from Windsurf on June 2, 2026, and it runs on macOS, Windows 10+ and Linux. Like Antigravity, it centers on agents rather than typing speed, and it supports ACP, the protocol Zed uses for external agents, so Codex, Claude Agent and OpenCode carry over.


**Key features:**


- The Agent Command Center, so you track local and cloud agents on one board.
- VS Code or Cursor settings import.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0, Pro $20/month and Max $200/month, while Teams, per Devin's billing docs, has an $80 monthly minimum, with full dev seats at $40/month each, for up to 100 users. Quotas refresh daily and weekly, but Cognition publishes no numbers for them.


**Pros:** the same ACP agents Zed runs, settings import from VS Code or Cursor, local and cloud agents on one board


**Cons:** an agent command center rather than an editor-speed play, unpublished quotas, an $80 monthly minimum on Teams


**Who it's for:** Teams that already run external agents through Zed and want one board for all of them.


**Final verdict:** Pick Devin Desktop if managing agents is now your main job and the editor is secondary.


### Two editors we left out


Kiro is built on Code OSS, like VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop, so it adds a workflow rather than a different editor trade. Void is archived on GitHub, which rules it out for anyone who wants updates.


## What Zed alternatives cost by price model


How you pay matters as much as how much, because a one-time license and a monthly AI plan age differently. The table starts with Zed's own plans as the baseline.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Read down the AI column and the entry prices cluster: Zed Pro and Copilot Pro both cost $10/month, Cursor Plus costs $8 but limits you to Cursor and Grok models, and Devin Desktop Pro costs $20. Zed Pro also lets you set an optional spending cap.


## Pros and cons of switching from Zed


The upside of moving to one of the alternatives to Zed depends on which gap pushed you, and the choosing guide below matches each gap to a pick.


The downsides are just as specific. Zed's collaboration is built in, while VS Code needs the Live Share extension and Sublime Text lists no real-time collaboration at all. VS Code runs on Electron and Cursor sits on its codebase, so moving to either gives up some of the native speed you had.


AI is the mixed one. Zed's free plan lets you bring your own keys and run external agents over ACP, including Claude Agent, Codex, OpenCode and Cursor, while Antigravity's IDE and Cursor Plus don't accept your own keys, and Antigravity's CLI takes only a Gemini key. One[Reddit thread](https://www.reddit.com/r/ZedEditor/comments/1tgcahd/how_decent_is_zed_as_a_vscode_replacement/) includes a user saying Zed's external-agent UI lacked many slash commands and session controls such as forking a session, though that's one person's report.


Sometimes the gap isn't the editor at all. If the slow part is turning a design file into working front-end code, a new editor won't close it, because that's a job for a[design engineer](https://www.awesomic.com/design-engineer) who works in design and code.


## How hard is it to move off Zed?


Moving off Zed is mostly a keymap and extension job, and the order below keeps you from discovering a missing piece mid-sprint:


1. List every Zed extension and setting you actually use, then check each one exists on your target.
2. Pick your keymap next: Zed's Vim mode maps to Neovim or Lapce's built-in modal editing, and its Helix mode maps to Helix.
3. If your old VS Code setup is still on disk, let Cursor or Devin Desktop import its settings.
4. Move your AI keys, after confirming the target accepts them.
5. Open your largest project in the new editor and time how long it takes to become usable.


That last step matters more than any benchmark.[Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits/) , in "Response Times: The 3 Important Limits," puts the limit for a response to feel instantaneous at about 0.1 second, for keeping your flow of thought at about 1 second, and for holding attention at about 10 seconds. By that yardstick, a project that takes over 10 seconds to open has already lost your attention.


Terminal moves need one extra decision. Neither Neovim nor Helix ships an agent panel, so the simplest route to AI there is a CLI agent in a second terminal pane, such as Aider or one of[its alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/aider-alternatives) .


## Mistakes to avoid when picking a Zed replacement


Most bad switches come from testing the wrong thing, and each of the four mistakes below is cheap to avoid.


### Judging speed on the wrong machine


The Windows slowdown in the Reddit report above didn't show up on Linux. Test on the OS and hardware you'll actually use, with your real project, not a demo folder.


### Treating an AI-first IDE as a faster editor


Cursor, Antigravity and Devin Desktop are agent tools first, and Cursor and Devin Desktop are both built on Code OSS. Comparing their model access and request limits is a separate decision from an editor trade, and the[Cursor alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/cursor-alternatives) roundup is built around that question.


### Skipping the admin questions


Zed's missing SSO can push a team out, but we didn't compare the other tools' SSO terms here, so read each business plan before you assume single sign-on is covered.


### Ignoring release dates


Lapce is still pre-1.0, and Helix's last tagged release is from July 2025, though both repos were updated in the past two months. Neither fact rules them out, but know the dates before your team standardizes on one.


## How to choose the right Zed alternative


Start from the reason you're leaving, because the alternatives to Zed each answer a different one:


- If you miss extensions, go back to VS Code.
- If you want native speed without AI, try Sublime Text or Lapce.
- If you live in a terminal, pick Neovim for full control or Helix for little setup.
- If you write Java or Kotlin, choose a JetBrains IDE.
- If the agent panel was your favorite part, compare Cursor, Antigravity and Devin Desktop.


And if heavy builds, not typing, are what strain your laptop, we built Awesomic to run that work on a cloud computer instead. Team size changes the math too, so a five-person team should price seats on every tool, ours included, because our Terms add Seat fees from $19.99 per teammate a month. If the backlog grows because you're short on developers, no editor clears it, and comparing[unlimited web development](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/unlimited-web-development-vs-freelancers-ship-3x-faster) with freelancers is the more useful step.


## Picking your next editor this week


Shortlist two Zed alternatives from the section above and give each one two working days on your real project, including a stretch of fixing and reworking code, the kind of task where the latency study found lag hurt more than in plain typing.


## FAQ


### What is the best free Zed alternative?


The answer depends on what you want to keep, since eight of the nine Zed editor alternatives here have a $0 option. VS Code is free with Copilot's Free plan of 2,000 completions a month, Lapce is free and the closest native match, Neovim and Helix are free terminal editors, and IntelliJ IDEA keeps its core features free after the Ultimate trial.


### Does Zed still have a free plan?


Yes. The Personal plan costs $0 and still lets you use your own API keys, external agents and other providers' predictions, but Zed's hosted models and Edit Predictions now need Pro at $10/month, which includes $5 of tokens and comes with a 14-day trial that needs no card. Verified university students aged 18+ get Pro free for one year, with $10 a month of token credits.


### Which editor is most similar to Zed?


Lapce is the closest. Like Zed, it's a native Rust editor that draws its interface on the GPU, it has remote development built in, and it's free under Apache-2.0, though it's still pre-1.0.


### Does Zed run on Windows?


Yes, since October 15, 2025. It needs a DirectX 11 GPU, supports WSL and SSH remoting, and ships builds for both x64 and Arm64 machines. If you leave, of the nine editors here, VS Code, Neovim, IntelliJ IDEA, Cursor, Google Antigravity and Devin Desktop also publish Windows ARM64 builds; Sublime Text, Lapce and Helix list x64 only.


### Can I keep Vim keybindings if I leave Zed?


Yes. Neovim is the obvious choice, Lapce has modal editing built in, and Helix uses its own modal model built on multiple selections, which Zed's Helix mode follows. If you're coming from Vim and pick Helix, expect to relearn some keys.
